Now that is amazing to hear. What is it if you don't mind me asking? I'm doing Web Development and want that to grow but I have a hard time figuring out low budget ways to market myself. I don't think I'm putting in nearly enough effort though so that's probably why.

I have a cleaning business. Started out only doing residential, now we do both residential and commercial. I spend maybe $200-300 a year on marketing (website, business cards and some little silent auction donations). So, totally different fields, BUT we both provide services, so maybe I can help.

The first year, I used the website Thumbtack to build a small base (20 residential clients - enough for me to pay my bills). Thumbtack is a bidding service for small business/self-employed; a person submits a bid looking for the kind of work you do, you see what they want, and you pay a few bucks to submit a bid (it used to be $5 or so for cleaning services, but they raised rates at the beginning of this year). The person requesting sees the first five bids and picks who they want - they offer this for web development services (just checked). As long as you can write a good pitch, you'll get 40% or so of the jobs you bid for - PM me for that, because I figured out a good format to get people to at least call nearly every time.

Then, I use referral discounts for residential clients. Some of those Thumbtack customers told their friends and neighbors, and I built my business up that way. I had a FB page, but that didn't really do much so I deleted it. I also got a website as soon as possible to appear more professional and tweaked SEO stuff - I land one client through google and the site is paid for for the year. I built up the commercial side this year because companies were just googling and I was the top result (luckily). I got property management companies by emailing them, or residential clients referred us to them.

Most services are best advertised via word-of-mouth. There is a very successful lawyer in town who is noted for saying he refuses to advertise, because advertising is for those who aren't making any money. I took his advice - none of those mailer coupons, fliers, TV/radio ads, and the company has an "exclusivity" vibe because of it (also, we're really good and offer more than the competition I guess - I don't worry about competition). I also made a deal with a couple of service people in different fields. They usually deal with the wealthy and if they passed my company's name along and we got the client, I would go clean their house for free. Because of this, and I think partly because we're small and local, we've landed some pretty big-name clients - retired pro athletes, people at the top of their field (architects, lawyers, bankers, business owners) and those people refer us to their family members. I don't do the free cleaning thing anymore really, now I pay quarterly bonuses to employees for every job they help land, like referrals from clients they work for or when they close a deal on an estimate.

Expand your network as much as possible because you never know who can offer help (some of my clients have offered various services or referrals to CPA's/law firms for incorporating, etc.). Like, tell everyone what you do for a living - plumbers, electricians, cashiers you deal with regularly, basically anyone in any job who you do regular business with. Actually, you may have more luck with people in trades at first. Most are nearing retirement age, and may still want a residual income, and if you help with web development, they can hire people to do the extra work/work for them when they're ready to retire. At least around here, most local tradesmen don't have a website or know anything about web development. AND, they're in other peoples' homes all the time, they'll refer you to various people any chance they can if you give them a fair deal and do good work.

So, word-of-mouth, doing the best work your can and owning your mistakes are the best way to establish yourself. I started out making $30 a week, and we're looking to finish this year at $170k (I know it's not much, but not too shabby). I had to use credit cards and savings to pay bills for a while, and didn't even have any real equipment. If you can, just keep the business in your home for as long as possible to keep the budget low (bonus: if you use 30% or less of your home, you can write that off - mortgage & utility use - at tax time). When you're not working on a project, look for ways to save money or promote your business (emailing potential clients). As soon as you can, get licensed by your city and file articles of incorporation with the state. It will give an air of professionalism compared to others who are at your level. Basically, work your ass off.

Accountanator Beta is a double-entry accounting spreadsheet that is totally free and works in google drive. It will tell you when you've made a mistake, has all the categories laid out for you, and will instantly generate a profit/loss statement and everything you need for taxes. This is what I used until I could afford accounting. Quickbooks Online is also good, because it produces little graphs to see how your business is growing, but it costs $$ (I think $30/month).

Don't join those business networking groups, it's usually a bunch of other broke people trying to sell you whatever they've got. As far as paying for advertising, work with private schools (can advertise in their sports calendars, yearbooks, etc.). Most business owners send their kids to private schools in my experience. Call churches in your area and ask to advertise in their little weekly newsletters, maybe? Oh yeah, and practice active listening when meeting with clients/potential clients. Personability and good communication will help immensely.

Well, that was super-long. I hope this helps, and good luck! We need more small businesses! It seems overwhelming, but you can do it!
